metadata.title: Agostini v. Felton, 521 U.S. 203 (1997) (No. 96-552)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Agostini v. Felton

Opinion filed: 1997-06-23

Docket No.: 96-552

Citations:
• 138 L. Ed. 2d 391
• 117 S. Ct. 1997
• 521 U.S. 203
• 1997 U.S. LEXIS 4000

Case holding summaries:
• concluding that program of sending public LAMBETH v. BD. OF COMM’RS 11 school teachers into parochial schools to provide remedial education to disadvantaged children did not result in excessive entanglement
• "We do not acknowledge, and we do not hold, that other courts should conclude our more recent cases have, by implication, overruled an earlier precedent."
• reminding appellate courts that "the views of five Justices that [a] case should be reconsidered or overruled cannot be said to have effected a change in Establishment Clause law"
• Court of Appeals erred in adhering to law of the case doctrine despite intervening Supreme Court precedent
• upholding programs employing public employees to provide remedial instruction and guidance counseling to nonpublic school children at sites away from the nonpublic school
• only one student sought state tuition assistance for religious education
• aid issued to students reached religious institution "only as a result of the genuinely independent and private choices of aid recipients"
• cautioning against entertaining successive appeals of legal questions open to dispute in an initial appeal, and observing that tolerance of such appeals would allow parties, inter alia, to "`speculate on chances from changes in [a court's] members' "
• sustaining New York law loaning secular textbooks to all children
• provision of diagnostic tests to religious schools provides only an incidental benefit
• involving a program giving "direct cash reimbursement" to religious schools for performing certain state-mandated tasks
• consent decree should be vacated under Rule 60(b) in light of amendments to the Railway Labor Act
• no excessive entanglement where State conducts annual audits to ensure that categorical state grants to religious colleges are not used to teach religion
• warning against transformation of Rule 60(b) "modification procedure into an impermissible avenue of collateral attack"
• sustaining section of IDEA providing all "disabled" children with necessary aid
• upholding neutrally available program because it did not "creat[e a] financial incentive for students to undertake sectarian education"
• "[T]he mere circumstance that [an aid recipient] has chosen to use neutrally available state aid to help pay for [a] religious education [does not] confer any message of state endorsement of religion"
• sustaining Washington law granting all eligible blind persons vocational assistance
• "[A]nguish, hardship and bitter strife" result "when zealous religious groups struggl[e] with one another to obtain the Government's stamp of approval"
• upholding neutrally available IDEA aid because it "creates no financial incentive for parents to choose a sectarian school"
• sign-language interpreter must transmit exactly what is said
• "Although Establishment Clause jurisprudence is characterized by few absolutes, the Clause does absolutely prohibit government-financed or government-sponsored indoctrination into the beliefs of a particular religious faith"
• stare decisis may yield where a prior decision's "underpinnings [have been] eroded, by subsequent decisions of this Court"
• "The general rule of long standing is that the law announced in the Court's decision controls the case at bar"
• applying a more stringent standard for recognizing changes in the law and "new rules" in light of the "interests of comity" present in federal habeas corpus proceedings
• "[T]he court cannot be required to disregard significant changes in law or facts if it is satisfied that what it has been doing has been turned through changed circumstances into an instrument of wrong" (internal quotation marks omitted)
• concluding that Equal Access Act has a secular purpose
• original decision issued June 11, 1956; rehearing granted Nov. 5, 1956
• noting that a "later development of . . . constitutional law" is a basis for overruling a decision
• overruling decision relied upon by Court of Appeals and reversing the lower court's judgment that relied upon the overruled case
• concluding that Adolescent Family Life Act had a secular purpose
• finding no "`symbolic link' " when Congress made federal funds neutrally available for adolescent counseling
• injunction should have been vacated in light of Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Bd. of Ed., 402 U. S. 1 (1971)
• no excessive entanglement where government reviews the adolescent counseling program set up by the religious institutions that are grantees, reviews the materials used by such grantees, and monitors the program by periodic visits
• observing that a decision is properly overruled where "development of constitutional law since the case was decided has implicitly or explicitly left [it] behind as a mere survivor of obsolete constitutional thinking"
• "The provision of benefits to so broad a spectrum of groups is an important index of secular effect"
• striking down Louisiana law that required creationism to be discussed with evolution in public schools because the law lacked a legitimate secular purpose
• sustaining local ordinance authorizing all parents to deduct from their state tax returns the costs of transporting their children to school on public buses
• invalidating Pennsylvania program on entanglement grounds because excessive monitoring would be required for the State to be certain that public school officials do not inculcate religion
• even “if a precedent of this Court . . . appears to rest on reasons rejected in some other line of decisions, the Court of Appeals should follow the case which directly controls, leaving to this Court the prerogative of overruling its own decisions.”
• stating that "excessive entanglement" has sometimes been considered independently, and sometimes as part of the "effects" analysis
• acknowledging that some interaction between church and state is inevitable and that some involvement between the two has always been tolerated
• invalidating Rhode Island program on entanglement grounds because "[a] comprehensive, discriminating, and continuing state surveillance will inevitably be required to ensure that th[e] restrictions [against indoctrination] are obeyed"
• distinguishing, for Establishment Clause purposes, books provided by the State to students from teachers paid by the State
• "[W]e cannot ignore here the danger that pervasive modern governmental power will ultimately intrude on religion . . ."
• "[T]eachers have a substantially different ideological character from books [and] [i]n terms of potential for involving some aspect of faith or morals in secular subjects, a textbook's content is ascertainable, but a teacher's handling of a subject is not"
• "Entanglement must be `excessive' before it runs afoul of the Establishment Clause."
• noting “[i]nteraction between church and state is inevitable”
• “Intervening developments in the law by themselves rarely constitute the extraordinary circumstances required for relief under Rule 60(b)(6), the only remaining avenue for relief on this basis from judg- ments lacking any prospective component.”
• suggesting that the effects and entanglement prongs of Lemon focus on substantially the same factors
